title: Seven Habits That Support Fertility
hook: Most fertility advice online is invented. NPR's illustrated guide sticks to what the evidence supports — and notably, half of it applies to the male partner.
key_points: Fertility is a shared matter: sperm quality contributes to roughly half of cases.
A whole-food, Mediterranean-style diet is the eating pattern with the most support.
Regular moderate exercise helps; extreme training can suppress fertility.
Smoking, heavy drinking, and cannabis all reduce fertility in both partners.
Sleep and stress management matter through their effect on reproductive hormones.
Timing intercourse to the fertile window beats trying to hit a single ovulation day.
content_html: Trying to conceive puts people in one of the internet's least trustworthy neighborhoods, where confident advice about specific foods, positions, and supplements vastly outnumbers anything actually studied. NPR's illustrated guide is useful mostly for what it leaves out: it sticks to habits with real evidence behind them.
extra_html:
The framing worth carrying away is that fertility is a shared project. Sperm quality contributes to roughly half of cases, so the diet, alcohol, smoking, and exercise advice applies to both partners — not, as it's often presented, to the person who would carry the pregnancy. The dietary pattern with the most support is the unglamorous one: whole foods, Mediterranean-style, rather than any single fertility superfood.

The rest is consistent with general health advice, which is itself informative. Moderate exercise helps and extreme training loads can suppress fertility. Smoking, heavy drinking, and cannabis reduce it in both partners. Sleep and stress act through reproductive hormones. And on timing, aiming for the fertile window — the several days up to and including ovulation — works better than trying to hit one exact day. None of this replaces seeing a clinician if you've been trying for a year, or six months over 35.

related.title: Contraception Options
related.hook: There's no single 'best' contraception — only the one that fits your body, your life, and your plans. Knowing the main types helps you choose well.

related.title: Building a Balanced Plate
related.hook: Forget counting every calorie — the simplest healthy-eating tool is a picture of a plate: half produce, a quarter grains, a quarter protein.

related.title: Alcohol and Your Health
related.hook: There's no amount of alcohol proven to be good for you — but there's a meaningful difference between a glass with dinner and patterns that quietly raise your risk of cancer, liver disease, and more.

related.title: How Much Exercise You Actually Need
related.hook: The headline number is smaller than most people fear: about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — roughly 20-some minutes a day — moves the needle on your health.

flashcards.prompt: Whose habits matter for a couple's fertility?
flashcards.back_html: Both partners'. Sperm quality contributes to roughly half of fertility difficulties, so diet, drinking, smoking, and exercise advice applies to the male partner too.

flashcards.prompt: Which statement about exercise and fertility matches the evidence?

choices.text: Regular moderate exercise helps, but extreme training can suppress fertility
Exercise has no measurable effect either way

flashcards.explanation_html: The relationship is a curve, not a line — moderate activity supports reproductive health while very high training loads can disrupt the hormones that drive it.

flashcards.prompt: What's the better way to think about timing?
flashcards.back_html: Aim for the fertile window — the several days leading up to and including ovulation — rather than trying to pinpoint one exact day.
